claims.text: A physics-informed machine-learning surrogate can integrate atomistic-simulation outputs with experimental conductivity measurements for HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly representing intrinsic defects and oxygen-induced disturbances will reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least 50% relative to analytical perfect-crystal models.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr in the 0–200 K regime can be represented by a nearly defect-free specimen state.
The 300–1200 K regime is represented by bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen addition.
A Gaussian Process Regression model will be trained on a combined atomistic-simulation and experimental dataset and augmented with physics-informed constraints.
Defect density and oxygen concentration will be model inputs used to represent nonlinear charge-scattering dependencies.
Training, cross-validation, and testing will span 0–200 K for nominally oxygen-free material and 300–1200 K for material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Intrinsic point defects and oxygen-induced microstructural distortions together form an effective defect landscape.
The effective defect landscape changes the distribution of energy barriers governing electron hopping and scattering.
Atomistic simulations can supply detailed scattering information, while experimental data can calibrate conductivity predictions.
Physics-informed constraints will keep the learned relations consistent with established defect and scattering theories.
The model will predict conductivity with less than 7% error near 150 K for the nominally oxygen-free specimen and near 850 K for the oxygen-containing specimen.
The model's prediction error will be at least 50% lower than that of conventional analytical approaches.
Analytical perfect-crystal models typically have greater than 14% conductivity error for real, defect-laden HfNbTaTiZr.
The approach is applicable only over 0–200 K for nominally oxygen-free samples and 300–1200 K for samples containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Prediction validity depends critically on how representative the simulation and experimental training data are.
Incomplete defect coverage in the training data may cause overfitting, and extrapolation outside the stated temperature ranges may be unreliable.
Conductivity measurements near 150 K and 850 K will be withheld from training and used as independent prediction benchmarks.
Deviation greater than 20% from the held-out conductivity measurements at the designated benchmark temperatures will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The low-temperature nominally oxygen-free specimen is variously described as nearly defect-free, as having intrinsic defects that must be modeled, and as defect-dominated. These are materially different defect states and are not reconciled.
